name: Money maxxing / career maxxing

card.summary: The idea that income and career success can offset or replace looks; supported in part by mate-preference research, untested as a strategy.
card.note: Evidence concerns status and attractiveness generally, not the strategy itself.

quick.overview:
Money maxxing and career maxxing refer to pursuing income and professional success as a route to status and attractiveness, as an alternative or addition to improving looks.

Reference works report that status and resources influence mate preferences and that looks affect career opportunities, but the strategy has not been tested directly.
quick.mechanism: The theory is that wealth and achievement raise perceived status, which influences attraction and also funds appearance improvements.
quick.risks: No direct health risks. Outcomes vary by person and culture, and research findings are correlational.

lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing are looksmaxxing-community terms for building income, wealth and professional standing, usually as a complement to improving appearance. Members present money as a way to pay for grooming, skincare, clothing and cosmetic procedures, and as an independent source of attractiveness.[1][4]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes a person's "sexual market value" as combining looks with perceived status and wealth, and notes that status or finances can be a way of out-competing others in social settings.[4] Research summarized in Wikipedia reports that women's mate preferences track status cues such as resources and dominance, and that perceived attractiveness can affect how people are judged for employment.[1]

The practice is described in community posts rather than in studies of the strategy itself. A forum post by a 16-year-old, for instance, describes shifting attention from looksmaxxing to making money once appearance goals were met.[5]

chain: Earn more income or advance in a career
Pay for grooming, skincare, clothing and procedures
Better-kept appearance plus the status cues that influence attraction
angle.text: Income can pay for the things that improve looks directly, such as skincare, haircuts, wardrobe, dental work and cosmetic procedures. Community members also say wealth and career status raise attractiveness on their own, a view that research on mate preferences partly echoes.

infobox: Looksmaxxing spaces; term coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and popularized on TikTok in the 2020s (looksmaxxing generally)[4]

paras: Status is the relative social value attributed to a person, and socioeconomic status is typically indexed by income, education and occupational prestige.[2] Reference works report that women's preferences for male partners track status cues such as resources and dominance, and that attractiveness affects hiring and social opportunities.[1] One finding cited on Wikipedia reports that men with a higher salary were perceived as more attractive to women, and another study found a positive correlation between facial symmetry and salary among American football quarterbacks.[1] Evolutionary psychologists describe prestige as an important component of male attractiveness alongside dominance.[3]

Forum members describe money maxxing as a way to afford grooming, procedures and clothing, and as an independent source of attractiveness. Others dispute how much money can offset looks.[5] Threads on the topic cover side jobs, investing and business ideas, and members ask whether starting college or a career later than peers matters. These are community positions, not research findings.
Wikipedia describes the community's "sexual market value" framework, in which looks combine with perceived status and wealth.[4]
No studies found. Economics and psychology literature on attractiveness and income exists but does not evaluate money maxxing as a practice.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, money maxxing is discussed as a second track beside looks, with members trading income ideas and debating whether wealth can offset or amplify appearance.[5]

claims.claim: Money can offset or replace looks in attraction
claims.believers: Proponents say wealth and career status raise perceived value, and that income also buys the grooming and procedures that improve appearance.[5]
claims.experts: Research summarized on Wikipedia reports that women's mate preferences track status and resource cues and that higher-salaried men were rated more attractive; these are correlational findings and do not test money maxxing as a strategy.[1]

claims.believers: Members describe spending earnings on skincare, clothing, dental work and cosmetic procedures once they have income.[5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested income as a driver of appearance outcomes within looksmaxxing; general research notes attractiveness can affect employment and social opportunities.[1]
